entities.evidence: The opening clause identifies Abraham as Isaac’s father.
Abraham fathers Isaac, whose name recurs as the subject of the next clause.
Abraham’s son Isaac now fathers Jacob.
Isaac fathers Jacob, the patriarch also called Israel.
The Jacob just named as Isaac’s son now fathers Judah and his brothers.
The final clause identifies Judah and his brothers as sons of the patriarch Jacob.

analysis.evidence: The opening clause אַבֿרָהָמ אַולֵדֿ לִאיסחָק says that Abraham fathered Isaac. Isaac then becomes the subject of the same verb in the next clause, confirming the father-to-son sequence.
analysis.morphology: Masculine singular personal name, without prefix or suffix, serving as the subject of אַולֵדֿ.
analysis.sense: Abraham, the patriarch who fathered Isaac.

analysis.evidence: In אַבֿרָהָמ אַולֵדֿ לִאיסחָק, Abraham is the subject and ל־ marks Isaac as the object. The genealogy then repeats the same verb with Isaac as the father of Jacob.
analysis.morphology: Aphel perfect, third person masculine singular, with no pronominal suffix

draft.change: Add a personal-name article for Syriac אִיסחָק and link it to the laughter root represented in the Hebrew spelling יִשְׂחָק.
draft.definition: The Syriac personal name of Abraham’s son Isaac, who fathered Jacob.
draft.evidence: Matthew 1:2 identifies Isaac by naming his father and his son. The unprefixed form in the second clause supplies the dictionary form.

analysis.evidence: Abraham is the subject of אַולֵדֿ and לִאיסחָק names the son he fathered. The next clause repeats the name without the prefix, אִיסחָק, as the subject who fathered Jacob.
analysis.morphology: Masculine singular personal name with prefixed לִ־ marking the direct object of אַולֵדֿ, “fathered.”
analysis.sense: Isaac, Abraham’s son and Jacob’s father

draft.change: Use the same isaac-syriac personal-name draft as position 2.
draft.definition: The Syriac personal name of Abraham’s son Isaac, who fathered Jacob.
draft.evidence: Matthew 1:2 identifies Isaac by naming his father and his son. The unprefixed form in the second clause supplies the dictionary form.

analysis.evidence: Abraham fathers לִאיסחָק in the first clause. The next clause repeats the name without לִ־ in אִיסחָק אַולֵדֿ ליַעקֻובֿ (“Isaac fathered Jacob”), making Isaac the subject and Jacob his son.
analysis.morphology: Masculine singular personal name, unprefixed, serving as the subject of אַולֵדֿ (“fathered”).
analysis.sense: Isaac, Abraham’s son and Jacob’s father

analysis.evidence: In אִיסחָק אַולֵדֿ ליַעקֻובֿ, Isaac is the subject and ל־ marks Jacob as the object. Isaac fathered Jacob.
analysis.morphology: Aphel perfect, third person masculine singular

draft.change: Add a name article for the Syriac spelling יַעקֻובֿ, with the same root link as the Hebrew name יַעֲקֹב.
draft.definition: יַעקֻובֿ is the Syriac form of the personal name Jacob. In Matthew 1:2 it names the patriarch.
draft.evidence: Matthew 1:2 places יַעקֻובֿ between Isaac and Judah in the genealogy. The unprefixed repetition supplies the Syriac dictionary form.

analysis.evidence: In אִיסחָק אַולֵדֿ ליַעקֻובֿ, Isaac fathers Jacob. The next clause repeats the name without ל as its subject and says that Jacob fathered Judah and his brothers.
analysis.morphology: Masculine singular personal name with prefixed ל marking the direct object of אַולֵדֿ.
analysis.sense: Jacob the patriarch, son of Isaac and father of Judah.

draft.change: Add a name article for the Peshitta spelling יַעקֻובֿ, linked to the same root as Hebrew יַעֲקֹב.
draft.definition: The Syriac form of the personal name Jacob, borne here by the patriarch.
draft.evidence: Matthew 1:2 identifies Jacob by naming Isaac as his father and Judah and his brothers as his sons.

analysis.evidence: Isaac fathers ליַעקֻובֿ. The genealogy then repeats the name without ל in יַעקֻובֿ אַולֵדֿ לִיהֻודָֿא ולַאחַוה_י, making Jacob the father in the next clause.
analysis.morphology: Masculine singular personal name, unprefixed and unsuffixed, serving as the subject of אַולֵדֿ.
analysis.sense: Jacob the patriarch, son of Isaac and father of Judah and his brothers.

analysis.evidence: יַעקֻובֿ is the subject of אַולֵדֿ. The following לִיהֻודָֿא ולַאחַוה_י names Judah and his brothers as the children Jacob fathered.
analysis.morphology: Aphel perfect, third person masculine singular

draft.change: Add a name article for the Syriac spelling יהודא, corresponding to the Hebrew יהודה in the existing Judah article.
draft.definition: The Syriac personal name Judah, here borne by Jacob’s son.
draft.evidence: Matthew 1:2 names Judah and his brothers as sons of Jacob. Genesis 29:35 connects the Hebrew name with Leah’s declaration that she will praise Yahweh.

analysis.evidence: The verse repeats the same pattern for three generations. In the final clause Jacob is the father, and לִיהֻודָֿא names the son he begot. The following ולַאחַוה_י, “and his brothers,” groups Jacob’s other sons with Judah.
analysis.morphology: Masculine singular personal name with prefixed לִ־ marking the direct object of אַולֵדֿ.

analysis.evidence: Jacob is the subject of אַולֵדֿ ‘begot’. The repeated ל marks Judah and his brothers as coordinated objects. The suffix refers to Judah, identifying the other sons of Jacob as Judah’s brothers.
analysis.morphology: Masculine plural noun in the construct state with a third-person masculine singular possessive suffix, prefixed by the conjunction ו and the object marker ל.
